pages.title: 3.2% and 4.1%: Europe's prices cooled faster than the forecasts

3-2-and-4-1-europe-s-prices-cooled-faste.title: 3.2% and 4.1%: Europe's prices cooled faster than the forecasts
3-2-and-4-1-europe-s-prices-cooled-faste.dek: France and Spain published November's first price readings on Friday. Both came in well below what analysts had pencilled in, and in Spain the slowdown went beyond fuel.
3-2-and-4-1-europe-s-prices-cooled-faste.text: On Friday morning two statistics offices did more for the inflation debate than a week of speeches. France’s harmonised inflation rate was 3.2% in November, down from 3.7% in October, INSEE’s preliminary data showed [1]. A Reuters poll of 15 analysts had expected 3.6% [1]. The national index rose 2.9%, against 3.4% in October [1]. Spain’s INE put its flash HICP at 4.1%, eight tenths below October’s 4.9% [2]. The office names the cause plainly: fuel prices fell, where they had risen in November 2025, and clothing and footwear rose less than a year earlier [2]. Consumer prices fell 0.6% from October [2]. The detail that matters most is core inflation, which strips out unprocessed food and energy: it dropped five tenths to 2.6% [2]. FinanzaOnline notes that analysts had expected 3.2% for Spanish core and 4.7% for the headline [3]. The slowdown therefore did not stop at the petrol pump. French services inflation eased too, from 2.6% to 2.3% [3]. Traders, the Italian outlet reports, trimmed their bets on a December rate rise only slightly; a hike remains by far the most likely scenario priced in swaps [3]. That is the right temperament. Two countries are not the euro area, and a flash is an estimate, revised next month. Germany and Italy report on Monday, the euro area on Tuesday [3][4]. What you can take from Friday is smaller and sturdier than a forecast. The energy shock is passing through the price indexes in the order textbooks describe: fuel first, then the things that carry fuel. Nobody announced it. Two spreadsheets showed it. This is reporting, not investment advice.

149-5-billion-the-ai-boom-arrives-throug.title: $149.5 billion: the AI boom arrives through the port
149-5-billion-the-ai-boom-arrives-throug.dek: America's goods deficit widened sharply in October because it imported a record amount of machinery for data centres. Tariffs did not stop the containers.
149-5-billion-the-ai-boom-arrives-throug.text: The US goods trade deficit jumped 10.7%, or $14.4 billion, to $149.5 billion in October, the Census Bureau said on Friday [1]. Economists polled by Reuters had expected $133 billion [1]. Goods imports rose 6.1% to $365.3 billion, the highest since the series began in 1992 [1]. Capital goods led, up 8.5% on the month and 80.0% on the year [1]. The reason is not mysterious. Businesses are spending heavily on AI, and the buildout relies on imported equipment [1]. ‘Capital goods imports are surging, showing that AI doesn’t always lead to greater US economic growth,’ said Christopher Rupkey of FWDBONDS [1]. Goldman Sachs economists wrote that the import surge is one reason AI adds less to GDP than corporate spending suggests [1]. This week the administration also proposed new maximum rates of 20% to 40% on 14 major partners, including China, Japan and the EU [1]. Friday’s figures are the context the speeches leave out. The gap the tariffs are meant to close widened, because American firms chose to buy what they could not yet make. Invoices follow demand, not slogans. This is reporting, not investment advice.

minus-3-21-points-what-trade-took-from-t.title: Minus 3.21 points: what trade took from the quarter
minus-3-21-points-what-trade-took-from-t.dek: The US economy grew fast in the third quarter. Imports took a large slice back.
minus-3-21-points-what-trade-took-from-t.text: Trade subtracted 3.21 percentage points from US GDP growth in the third quarter, the government reported on Wednesday; the economy still grew at a 4.3% annualised rate, carried by consumer spending and AI-related equipment investment [1]. Trade has not added to growth for four straight quarters [1]. Inventory investment added 1.64 points in the third quarter [1]. The arithmetic is simple and stubborn: what a country buys abroad does not count as its own output, however modern the machine.

20-to-40-the-tariff-menu-for-14-partners.title: 20% to 40%: the tariff menu for 14 partners
20-to-40-the-tariff-menu-for-14-partners.dek: Washington proposed new maximum rates this week. Friday's trade data arrived as the counter-argument.
20-to-40-the-tariff-menu-for-14-partners.text: The Trump administration this week proposed new maximum potential rates of 20% to 40% on 14 major trading partners, including China, Japan and the European Union, to counter what the White House calls excess industrial capacity, Reuters reports [1]. On Friday the goods deficit came in at $149.5 billion, the widest since March 2025 [1]. Imports have risen quickly despite the duties [1]. A tariff schedule is a proposal. The import ledger is what happened.

milan-and-frankfurt-up-a-quiet-friday-cl.title: Plus 1.89% in Milan, plus 0.86% in Frankfurt: a quiet Friday close
milan-and-frankfurt-up-a-quiet-friday-cl.dek: Every main European index finished the week's last session higher, with Milan and Madrid ahead and Zurich behind. No speech moved it. The inflation figures did some of the work.
milan-and-frankfurt-up-a-quiet-friday-cl.text: Europe ended Friday the way it started Thursday: up. Boursorama’s levels after the cash close show Milan’s FTSE MIB up 1.89% at 49,275.60 and Madrid’s IBEX 35 up 1.72% at 19,386.60 [1]. The Euro Stoxx 50 gained 1.18%, Amsterdam’s AEX 1.24%, London’s FTSE 100 0.84% and the DAX 0.86% to 25,431.29 [1]. Paris rose 0.58% and Zurich’s SMI 0.58% [1]. Andreas Lipkow, writing for wallstreet:online, described investors as willing to buy German blue chips, ‘allerdings weiterhin sehr selektiv und nicht zu jedem Preis’ — very selectively, and not at any price [2]. Technology and carmakers stayed in demand [2]. He pointed to Friday’s US data: a wider goods trade deficit and stronger than expected wholesale inventories, which he reads as early signs of softer consumer momentum [2]. The level is the dull fact. The DAX ended Thursday at 25,215.52 and stood at 25,431.29 after Friday’s close, by Boursorama’s count [1]. The week ends with Milan and Madrid at the top of the table and every main index in the black. Breadth is a better sign than height. This is reporting, not investment advice.

selektiv-und-nicht-zu-jedem-preis-the-bu.title: 'Not at any price': the buyer's condition
selektiv-und-nicht-zu-jedem-preis-the-bu.dek: Frankfurt's Friday buyers wanted technology and cars, and they wanted them cheap.
selektiv-und-nicht-zu-jedem-preis-the-bu.text: Andreas Lipkow of wallstreet:online described Friday’s German buyers as selective and unwilling to pay any price [1]. Technology and carmakers stayed in demand: the first, he wrote, on hopes the AI trend continues, the second as dividend stories [1]. He read the day’s US trade and inventory data as hints of slower consumption and therefore of a cautious Fed [1]. The Census Bureau figures he referred to show wholesale inventories up 0.9% in October [2]. A selective buyer is a healthier market than an eager one. This is reporting, not investment advice.

new-york-trades-a-short-friday.title: Plus 1.27% at Europe's close: New York's short Friday
new-york-trades-a-short-friday.dek: Wall Street opened after Thanksgiving for a shortened session that closes after this edition goes out.
new-york-trades-a-short-friday.text: US markets reopened on Friday after Thursday’s holiday for a session that ends early, at 19:00 Berlin time. After Europe’s close, the S&P 500 was up 1.27% at 7,274.08 on Boursorama’s board, after 7,182.78 on Wednesday [1]. Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 had closed 2.11% higher at 58,711.11 [1]. These are intraday levels, not closing prices. Half-day sessions are thin; the move means less than the number suggests. This is reporting, not investment advice.

podium-vs-print-a-strategic-mistake-and-.title: Podium vs Print: 'a strategic mistake', and €1.582 trillion
podium-vs-print-a-strategic-mistake-and-.dek: Emmanuel Macron warned against cutting the EU's next budget. The paper on the table already is a cut, and four countries walked out over its size.
podium-vs-print-a-strategic-mistake-and-.text: The podium. France’s president said it would be ‘a strategic mistake’ to lower the EU’s long-term spending [1]. Countries such as France and Italy want a higher-spending budget; Germany leads those who want restraint [1]. The print. The Commission’s original proposal was €2tn [1]. The paper set up to break the impasse proposes cutting roughly €220bn to €230bn, and the budget under the current proposal totals €1.582tn, including €140bn to repay pandemic-era borrowing [1]. Four countries that want it smaller, among them Denmark and Austria, walked out after several hours [1]. The talks ended after 12 hours on Thursday without a deal [1]. Friedrich Merz spoke of ‘new movement’ but said ‘we are not there yet’ [1]. The gap. The podium argues about direction. The print has already moved: cuts of roughly €220bn to €230bn are on the table before a single vote [1]. Seven-year budgets need all 27 signatures, so the size that survives will be the size the most reluctant government can sign. Bulgaria, which had opposed the Ukraine loan, now says it will fund its non-military part [1]. That is what progress looks like in Brussels: one country, one half of one line. This is reporting, not investment advice.

she-has-not-been-elected-macron-answers-.title: 'She has not been elected': Macron answers Le Pen
she-has-not-been-elected-macron-answers-.dek: France's 2027 election walked into the budget room.
she-has-not-been-elected-macron-answers-.text: Marine Le Pen, frontrunner in France’s presidential race, called the budget talks ‘underhanded political manoeuvring to thwart the democratic will of the French people’, the BBC reports [1]. Last month she said she would significantly reduce French aid to Ukraine and EU contributions if elected [1]. Emmanuel Macron replied in Brussels that it is ‘an odd kind of arrogance’ to act as if she were already in charge, ‘because, as things stand, she has not been elected’ [1]. Many governments want the budget locked in before the 2027 elections [1]. That is the reason a seven-year plan is being argued about in a hurry.

12-hours-four-walk-outs-and-a-date-in-de.title: 12 hours, four walk-outs and a date in December
12-hours-four-walk-outs-and-a-date-in-de.dek: The EU's budget summit ended without a deal. The next attempt is already on the calendar.
12-hours-four-walk-outs-and-a-date-in-de.text: Talks on the EU’s 2028–2034 budget ended after 12 hours on Thursday, with four countries walking out after several hours, the BBC reports [1]. The European Council has called a two-day summit for 17 and 18 December [1]. Each country effectively holds a veto [1]. A missed deadline in Brussels is a scheduling fact, not a collapse.

february-2027-a-spanish-economist-for-fr.title: February 2027: a Spanish economist for Frankfurt
february-2027-a-spanish-economist-for-fr.dek: The summit's one completed decision was a name.
february-2027-a-spanish-economist-for-fr.text: Pablo Hernández de Cos was named as the next president of the European Central Bank, replacing Christine Lagarde from February 2027, the BBC reports [1]. It was the one decision the summit finished. Appointments are quieter than budgets, and usually last longer.

the-annex-4-8-13-loneliness-by-the-front.title: The Annex: 4%, 8%, 13%: loneliness by the front door
the-annex-4-8-13-loneliness-by-the-front.dek: England's housing survey asked people how often they feel lonely. The answer depends on whether you own, rent privately or rent from a social landlord.
the-annex-4-8-13-loneliness-by-the-front.text: The English Housing Survey for 2025-26, published on Thursday, asks household reference persons the standard national question: how often do you feel lonely [1]. Among owner occupiers, 4% said often or always [1]. Among private renters it was 8%, and among social renters 13% [1]. Within social housing, 15% of council tenants said so, against 12% of housing association tenants [1]. Owner occupiers were also likelier to say they never feel lonely: 38%, against 29% of private renters [1]. The survey is careful about what it does not claim. The link between well-being and tenure ‘could be mediated by related factors, such as income, age and working status’ [1]. Owning a home does not make you less lonely. People who own homes tend to be older, richer and more settled, and those things travel together. Two other lines deserve your attention. Across all tenures, mean anxiety stood at 3.0 out of 10 in 2025-26, against 2.7 before the pandemic [1]. And the share in each tenure who feel lonely often or always has stayed broadly the same since 2021-22 [1]. No surge, no recovery. A dull, steady number is still a number someone can work on, street by street.

94-82-75-who-likes-the-place-they-live.title: 94%, 82%, 75%: who likes the place they live
94-82-75-who-likes-the-place-they-live.dek: Satisfaction with one's home slipped a little since before the pandemic.
94-82-75-who-likes-the-place-they-live.text: In 2025-26, 94% of owner occupiers in England said they were satisfied with their accommodation, 82% of private renters and 75% of social renters [1]. Since 2019-20, satisfaction fell slightly among owners, from 95%, and among social renters, from 78% [1]. Across all tenures, life satisfaction averaged 7.5, against 7.7 before the pandemic [1]. Small declines measured carefully over years are more useful than large ones asserted loudly. These are the careful kind.

7-8-against-6-9-life-satisfaction-by-ten.title: 7.8 against 6.9: life satisfaction by tenure
7-8-against-6-9-life-satisfaction-by-ten.dek: England's housing survey also measured how satisfied people are with their lives.
7-8-against-6-9-life-satisfaction-by-ten.text: Owner occupiers in England scored a mean of 7.8 out of 10 for life satisfaction in 2025-26, private renters 7.3 and social renters 6.9, the English Housing Survey reports [1]. Anxiety ran the other way: 2.7, 3.4 and 3.6 [1]. Private renters’ life satisfaction rose from 7.1 in 2024-25 [1]. The survey warns that income, age and work may explain much of the gap [1].

191-77-for-saturday-the-cold-week-s-bill.title: €191.77 for Saturday: the cold week's power bill comes down
191-77-for-saturday-the-cold-week-s-bill.dek: Saturday's wholesale electricity in Germany costs more than a third less than Friday's, the dearest day since mid-November. Weekends still do what weekends do.
191-77-for-saturday-the-cold-week-s-bill.text: Friday’s day-ahead auction set Saturday’s German-Luxembourg electricity price at an average of €191.77 a megawatt hour, according to Energy-Charts data from the Bundesnetzagentur’s SMARD platform [1]. Friday itself averaged €301.82, the cold week’s dearest day [1]. Saturday’s quarter-hours run from €138.91 at 23:45 to €232.03 at 17:30 [1]. The fall is mostly the calendar. Offices and factories close, demand drops, and the expensive gas plants at the top of the merit order are needed less. It is not a turn in the energy shock. Brent crude futures traded at $96.60 a barrel on Friday afternoon and were set to snap a three-week losing streak, Reuters reported via RTÉ, after attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and on Saudi infrastructure [2]. Saudi Aramco’s Jazan refinery temporarily halted some operations after a projectile struck it on Thursday, killing a Nepali worker [2]. So the two numbers point in different directions for different reasons. Oil prices a war; Saturday’s power prices a weekend. You pay both, but only one of them you can shift by running the washing machine at night. This is reporting, not investment advice.

96-60-and-four-days-up-the-barrel-turns.title: $96.60 and four days up: the barrel turns
96-60-and-four-days-up-the-barrel-turns.dek: Oil was set to end a three-week slide as attacks on Gulf shipping and Saudi refineries continued.
96-60-and-four-days-up-the-barrel-turns.text: Brent crude futures traded at $96.60 a barrel on Friday afternoon, after four sessions of gains, and touched their highest since 9 November, Reuters reports via RTÉ [1]. WTI was at $85.14 [1]. Iran has continued to attack ships in the Strait of Hormuz, and Yemen’s Houthis have struck Saudi infrastructure, including Ras Tanura [1]. ANZ analysts think Brent can push above $100 without a major new escalation, but that ‘increasingly requires evidence of constrained deliverable supply’ [1]. OPEC+ meets on Sunday [1]. An analyst’s ‘can’ is not a price. It is a condition, and conditions are worth reading. This is reporting, not investment advice.

1-000-strikes-on-a-grid-ukraine-imports-.title: More than 1,000 strikes on a grid: Ukraine imports its light
1-000-strikes-on-a-grid-ukraine-imports-.dek: Ukraine stopped exporting electricity after 20 November.
1-000-strikes-on-a-grid-ukraine-imports-.text: Russia has carried out more than 1,000 strikes on Ukraine’s energy system since September, targeting generation and high-voltage substations, Euronews reports [1]. After the attack on 20 November Ukraine halted electricity exports, and imports reached their highest level since mid-June, according to the Centre for Economic Strategy [1]. On Friday engineers in Dnipropetrovsk carried out emergency shutdowns after voltage fell in the high-voltage grid [1]. Europe’s interconnectors are now part of Ukraine’s air defence.

2-6-the-core-number-spain-did-not-expect.title: 2.6%: the core number Spain did not expect
2-6-the-core-number-spain-did-not-expect.dek: Headline inflation falls when fuel falls. Core inflation falls when the rest of the economy follows.
2-6-the-core-number-spain-did-not-expect.text: Spain’s flash core inflation, excluding unprocessed food and energy, fell five tenths to 2.6% in November, INE said [1]. On the harmonised measure core stood at 2.7% [1]. FinanzaOnline reports that economists had expected 3.2% for core, which is why the outlet says the slowdown goes beyond energy [2]. Prices overall fell 0.6% on the month [1]. A flash is an advance figure, confirmed or revised next month [1]. Read it as a direction, not a verdict.

monday-14-00-tuesday-11-00-the-two-dates.title: Monday, then Tuesday: the two dates that follow
monday-14-00-tuesday-11-00-the-two-dates.dek: France and Spain went first. Germany, Italy and the euro area report next.
monday-14-00-tuesday-11-00-the-two-dates.text: Destatis lists its preliminary November consumer prices for Monday 30 November, published ‘im Laufe des Tages’ [2]. FinanzaOnline puts the time at 14:00 and reports that economists expect German harmonised inflation to slow to 2.7% from 2.9% [1]. Italy’s Istat reports the same morning, starting from 5.6% on the harmonised measure in October [1]. The euro-area flash follows on Tuesday 1 December, from 4% in October, with expectations of 3.9% to 4% [1]. Expectations are not data. On Monday you will have data.

ordinary-ledger-7-1-billion-on-the-holid.title: Ordinary Ledger: $7.1 billion on the holiday, 0.9% in the warehouse
ordinary-ledger-7-1-billion-on-the-holid.dek: Black Friday's headlines are forecasts. Friday's actual numbers were a holiday's online receipts and a month of stock on wholesalers' shelves.
ordinary-ledger-7-1-billion-on-the-holid.text: Three entries from the back office of the holiday season. $7.1 billion. US consumers spent about that much online on Thanksgiving Day, 10.4% more than last year, according to Adobe Analytics [1]. Adobe forecasts $12.9 billion for Black Friday itself, up 9.2% [1]. Reuters notes that most of the season’s projected gains will come from inflation, which at 3.8% runs about a percentage point above each of the last two years [1]. 82%. That is the share of consumers in a November survey by the National Retail Federation who said they were taking steps to manage holiday costs, such as buying cheaper gifts or buying for fewer people [2]. The NRF expects 182.7 million people to shop over the five days to Cyber Monday, against 186.9 million who did last year [2]. 0.9%. Wholesale inventories rose that much in October, after 0.8% in September; retail inventories rose 0.8% [3]. It is the least glamorous line of the day. It is also the one that decides whether January brings discounts or empty shelves. One shopper in Raleigh told Reuters he would only buy items discounted by at least 40% [1]. That is not a mood. It is a rule, and rules are what budgets are made of. This is reporting, not investment advice.

87-and-40-the-shopper-who-pays-later.title: 87% and 40%: the shopper who pays later
87-and-40-the-shopper-who-pays-later.dek: Participation in the five-day sales is the highest in a decade. Some of it will be paid for in instalments.
87-and-40-the-shopper-who-pays-later.text: Deloitte’s survey of 1,200 consumers found 87% planned to buy during the Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales, up from 82% in 2025, CNBC reports [1]. Shoppers expect to spend an average of $624, similar to last year [1]. Some 40% of Generation Z shoppers plan to use buy now, pay later [1]. Deloitte’s Brian McCarthy described people ‘feeling the squeeze on prices’ but ‘still wanting to protect the holidays’ [1]. Instalments are not a scandal. They are a bill with a later date. Write the date down.

15-1-billion-why-monday-still-wins.title: $15.1 billion: why Monday still wins
15-1-billion-why-monday-still-wins.dek: Black Friday gets the crowds. Cyber Monday gets the larger online receipts.
15-1-billion-why-monday-still-wins.text: Adobe expects Cyber Monday to remain the biggest online shopping day, with sales up 6.2% to $15.1 billion, Anadolu Agency reports [1]. Over the five days from Thanksgiving it forecasts $47.5 billion online, up 7.4% [1]. The NRF expects November-December holiday retail sales of $1.013 trillion, up 4.2% [1]. Oxford Economics expects 2.2% growth after inflation [1]. The gap between those two growth rates is the price level.

eight-principles-and-100-fake-reviewed-s.title: Eight principles and 100 fake-reviewed shops: Singapore reads the AI market
eight-principles-and-100-fake-reviewed-s.dek: Singapore's competition watchdog published a study of its AI market. It found no monopoly yet, and plenty of ordinary cheating made easier.
eight-principles-and-100-fake-reviewed-s.text: The Competition and Consumer Commission of Singapore released the findings of its AI Market Study on Friday [1]. Its main finding is reassuring: businesses generally have a good range of cloud providers and AI models and can switch between them [1]. The risks it names are specific. Dominant firms could favour their own products or restrict access to essential technologies; dominant AI agent providers could stop rival agents from working with other operating systems; and AI pricing tools could learn to coordinate prices ‘even without being explicitly instructed to do so’ [1]. The consumer section is the more concrete. CCS says that in 2026 it acted against a fake review provider that used generative AI to write reviews for about 100 businesses [1]. AI can also personalise dark patterns, such as false scarcity messages, to an individual’s online behaviour [1]. And as AI enters appliances and cars, the study asks for manual overrides and components ‘that cannot be overridden by AI’ [1]. Out of this come eight guiding principles, from pro-competitive algorithms to accuracy [1]. They are not a law. They are a regulator telling a market, in plain words, what it will look for. That is how most good rules begin.

false-scarcity-made-personal-the-dark-pa.title: 'False scarcity', made personal: the dark-pattern problem
false-scarcity-made-personal-the-dark-pa.dek: Singapore's regulator explains how AI makes an old sales trick harder to see.
false-scarcity-made-personal-the-dark-pa.text: Dark patterns are interface tricks that nudge people into choices against their interests. Singapore’s CCS says AI can personalise them, for example false scarcity messages tailored to a consumer’s online behaviour, and makes it easier to build websites that use such tactics [1]. The regulator admits the covert nature of some dark patterns ‘makes them difficult to detect and address’ [1]. In 2025 it found a car-detailing workshop had used ChatGPT to generate reviews for customers without their knowledge [1]. On a Black Friday, ‘only two left’ is worth reading twice.

80-0-a-year-the-machines-behind-the-chat.title: 80.0% a year: the machines behind the chatbots
80-0-a-year-the-machines-behind-the-chat.dek: AI's physical side shows up in customs data.
80-0-a-year-the-machines-behind-the-chat.text: US imports of capital goods rose 8.5% in October and 80.0% on the year, Reuters reports, citing the Census Bureau; the AI infrastructure buildout ‘is heavily reliant on imports’ [1]. Goldman Sachs economists say this is one reason AI adds less to GDP than corporate spending figures suggest [1]. Software is weightless. Data centres are not.

almost-80-in-a-week-england-s-flu-arrive.title: Almost 80% in a week: England's flu arrives early
almost-80-in-a-week-england-s-flu-arrive.dek: Flu admissions rose sharply across England, and nearly tripled in the South East. Hospitals are busy, and vaccine uptake among small children is lower than last year.
almost-80-in-a-week-england-s-flu-arrive.text: Flu hospital admissions across England rose by almost 80% in a week, and in the South East the rate almost tripled, according to the UK Health Security Agency [1]. The South West saw a rise of about a quarter [1]. ‘A lot of people think it’s not serious. It absolutely is,’ said Dr Suzanna McDonald of UKHSA [1]. Flu arrived ‘a few weeks ahead’ of last year, she said, but remains ‘very, very unpredictable’: last season also started early and peaked at moderate levels [1]. The hospitals feel it. More than 570 patients passed through the Royal Berkshire Hospital’s emergency department in a single 24-hour period last week, which its chief operating officer called ‘probably’ the second busiest day it had ever had [1]. RSV kept the children’s department busy too [1]. Some hospitals, including Queen Alexandra in Portsmouth, are encouraging masks in certain areas [1]. The weak line is uptake. Just over a third of two- and three-year-olds have had a flu vaccine, and uptake among young children and over-65s is lower than at the same point last year [1]. A GP in Oxfordshire noted that the vaccine needs a couple of weeks to take effect, so a jab now covers Christmas [1]. Health systems are built for winter. They work best when the appointments are kept.

214-million-for-malaria-vaccines-and-70-.title: $214 million for malaria vaccines, and 70% coverage
214-million-for-malaria-vaccines-and-70-.dek: A grant would let Gavi restore its support to 85% of eligible children in high-burden areas.
214-million-for-malaria-vaccines-and-70-.text: Gavi said on Friday it has received a grant of up to $214 million from GiveWell to sustain and expand malaria vaccination in Africa [1]. If approved by Gavi’s board in December, it would restore support to 85% of eligible populations in moderate- and high-transmission areas, after funding limits had cut planned support to 70% [1]. Sabin Vaccine Institute analysis finds three-dose coverage at 70% on average where the vaccine is being rolled out, and first-dose coverage at 80% [1]. Malaria vaccination is now routine in 25 African countries [1]. In 2024 there were an estimated 610,000 malaria deaths, around 74% of them children under five [1]. A grant is paperwork. Here the paperwork is doses.

a-third-of-toddlers-the-gap-in-england-s.title: A third of toddlers: the gap in England's flu defence
a-third-of-toddlers-the-gap-in-england-s.dek: Uptake among the youngest and oldest is running behind last year.
a-third-of-toddlers-the-gap-in-england-s.text: Just over a third of two- and three-year-olds in England have had a flu vaccine, UKHSA figures show, and uptake among young children and over-65s is lower than at the same point last year, the BBC reports [1]. School-age children who missed the nasal spray at school can get it at some pharmacies from 1 December [1]. Children carry flu home. A spray in December protects a grandparent at Christmas.

155-drones-110-down-and-no-power-to-expo.title: 155 drones, 110 down, and no power to export
155-drones-110-down-and-no-power-to-expo.dek: Russia's overnight attack hit rail, energy and homes in nine Ukrainian regions. Ukraine has stopped exporting electricity and is importing the most since June.
155-drones-110-down-and-no-power-to-expo.text: Since Thursday evening Russia launched 155 strike drones at Ukraine, 51 of them jet-powered, and Ukrainian air defences shot down 110, Euronews reports, citing the air force [1]. Prime Minister Sergey Koretsky said strikes hit the railway, the energy sector, civilian enterprises and homes in nine regions [1]. Two people were killed at an enterprise in Nizhyn, an 86-year-old woman in Izium and one person in Kryvyi Rih [1]. The figure behind the night is in the grid. After the attack on 20 November Ukraine completely halted electricity exports, and imports reached their highest since mid-June, according to the Centre for Economic Strategy [1]. Since September Russia has carried out more than 1,000 strikes on the energy system, including high-voltage substations [1]. Ukrainian drones in turn struck a Rosatom heat and power plant and a synthetic rubber plant in Yefremov, which Kyiv says makes solid rocket fuel components [1]. Zelenskyy said on Thursday night that Russia was preparing ‘a new mass strike’ and asked people to heed missile alarms [2]. Donald Trump wrote that he had asked Vladimir Putin to pull back ‘all Military aggression against territories throughout Europe’ [2]. The warning and the request arrived on the same night. Only one of them came with a count.

a-blood-bath-and-a-strong-possibility-th.title: 'A complete bloodbath' and 'a strong possibility': diplomacy by post
a-blood-bath-and-a-strong-possibility-th.dek: The US president described his talks with Putin on social media. Ukraine's air force described the night.
a-blood-bath-and-a-strong-possibility-th.text: Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social that he had spent ‘a lot of time’ with Vladimir Putin in China on pulling back military aggression in Europe, calling the war ‘A COMPLETE BLOODBATH’ and a quick deal ‘a strong possibility’, Al Jazeera reports [1]. He said he briefed NATO’s Mark Rutte at Mar-a-Lago on Wednesday [1]. The same night Russia struck Kyiv with ballistic missiles, wounding seven people [1]. Possibilities are announced; strikes are counted. Watch the count.

nearly-500-strikes-beyond-500-km-the-lon.title: Nearly 500 strikes beyond 500 km: the long war
nearly-500-strikes-beyond-500-km-the-lon.dek: Ukraine has struck deep into Russia more often this year than in all previous years combined.
nearly-500-strikes-beyond-500-km-the-lon.text: Ukraine launched nearly 500 strikes at Russian targets more than 500km away in 2026, more than in the first four years of the war combined, according to AFP analysis of ACLED data to 20 November, the Guardian reports [1]. Some targets were 1,500km from both sides [1]. Ukraine’s foreign minister expressed ‘regret’ over ‘unintended consequences’ of an attack on Russian ships in a Libyan port [1]. Range brings reach, and with reach comes responsibility for where the debris falls.

60-2-full-and-120-needed-england-s-droug.title: 60.2% full and 120% needed: England's drought outlasts the autumn
60-2-full-and-120-needed-england-s-droug.dek: Reservoirs are filling slowly, but England needs well above average rain all winter to leave drought by spring. The weekly report is a lesson in patient accounting.
60-2-full-and-120-needed-england-s-droug.text: England’s reservoirs held 60.2% of their capacity on 24 November, up on the week, the Environment Agency’s weekly drought report says [1]. Fourteen reservoirs or groups remain less than 50% full, eight of them classed as exceptionally low [1]. Severe drought persists in parts of Cornwall, Devon, Dorset, Somerset and East and West Sussex, areas that rely on Ardingly and Wimbleball reservoirs [1]. The sentence that matters is a requirement, not a forecast: ‘We need at least 120% of average rainfall over the next 5 months for the entire country to be out of drought by the spring’ [1]. Last week rain totals ranged from 49mm in the south-west to 11mm in the east, and river flows fell at more than three-quarters of reported sites [1]. Groundwater fell at most sites because dry soils delay recharge [1]. Farmers feel it first. Many irrigation reservoirs began the refill season at historic lows, and there are 386 restrictions on abstraction licences, down from 431 the week before [1]. The agency is advising the sector to act now in case drought runs into spring [1]. It is unglamorous work: permits, licences, lock closures on canals. It is also how a country keeps the taps on without anyone noticing.

82-mph-in-mantoloking-the-flood-after-th.title: 82 mph in Mantoloking: the flood after the feast
82-mph-in-mantoloking-the-flood-after-th.dek: Storms on America's east coast cut power to nearly a million customers and postponed a parade for the first time.
82-mph-in-mantoloking-the-flood-after-th.text: Heavy rain and high winds swept the US east coast on Thanksgiving, cutting power to nearly a million customers at the peak and leading to water rescues from New York to Virginia, the Guardian reports [1]. New Jersey saw flooding at levels not seen since Hurricane Sandy in 2012; the strongest gust, 82 mph, was measured in Mantoloking [1]. Macy’s postponed its parade for the first time [1]. St Louis had 7.3 inches of snow, and freeze warnings cover parts of the Deep South [1]. ‘The bulk of the storm impacts are behind us, but tidal flooding will continue today,’ the National Weather Service said on Friday [1]. Clean-up is the part of weather that never trends.

386-licences-restricted-the-farm-side-of.title: 386 licences restricted: the farm side of a dry year
386-licences-restricted-the-farm-side-of.dek: England's drought is now counted in abstraction licences and canal closures.
386-licences-restricted-the-farm-side-of.text: There are 386 restrictions on abstraction licences in England, down from 431 a week earlier, the Environment Agency reports [1]. Seven navigation closures and four restrictions remain on the Canal & River Trust network [1]. Confirmed drought incidents total 440 this year, with no new ones in the last two weeks [1]. Every one of those numbers is a form someone filed. That is how adaptation looks up close.
